title: Priming Sugar Calculator 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
h1: Priming Sugar for Home Beer Carbonation
description: Calculate priming sugar (grams) for homebrew bottle conditioning. Inputs: volume, target CO2, fermentation temp. Supports dextrose, table sugar, DME, honey.
intro:
**Priming sugar** is the small, measured dose of fermentable sugar you add to fully fermented beer right before bottling, so the residual yeast in suspension produces CO2 inside the sealed bottle and carbonates the beer naturally. This process is called **bottle conditioning** and has been the traditional method for centuries, dating back to the early Belgian Trappist breweries and to pre-industrial English cask and bottle ales.

The amount of sugar required depends on three variables: the **volume of beer** being bottled (in liters), the **target CO2 volumes** for the beer style (a unit equal to volumes of dissolved CO2 per volume of beer at standard temperature and pressure), and the **peak fermentation temperature**, which determines how much CO2 is already dissolved in the beer at the moment of bottling. Beer fermented warm holds less residual CO2 than beer fermented cold, so warm-fermented batches need more priming sugar to reach the same target.

This calculator uses the standard formula popularized by **John Palmer** in *How to Brew* and validated by the Brewers Association and BJCP style guidelines. It accepts four sugar types: **dextrose (corn sugar)** — the homebrewer standard, fully fermentable, neutral flavor, factor 3.86 g/L per volume; **table sugar (sucrose)** — 91% as efficient as dextrose due to a slight conversion penalty, factor 3.51; **dry malt extract (DME)** — adds residual sweetness and a touch of body, factor 4.50; and **honey** — adds a slight floral note, factor 4.26 (less fermentable than dextrose, ~75-80% efficient).

The target CO2 volumes vary widely by style: **British cask ales** sit at 1.0-1.5 volumes (almost flat by US standards), **American ales and IPAs** at 2.2-2.7, **German pilsners and continental lagers** at 2.4-2.7, **wheat beers and hefeweizens** at 3.3-4.5, and **Belgian tripels, saisons and lambics** at 3.0-4.5. Over-priming a standard 12 oz bottle past 4 volumes risks **bottle bombs**: the glass can shatter from internal pressure. Use proper Belgian or champagne bottles rated for higher pressure for any style above 3.5 volumes.

Enter your batch volume, target CO2 volumes, peak fermentation temperature, and chosen sugar type. The calculator returns the exact grams to add, the residual CO2 already in solution, an ounce equivalent for US homebrewers, and a safety recommendation for your selected pressure level.
keyTakeaway: **6–8 g/L dextrose for standard beers (2.4 vol CO₂)**. Belgians 9–10 g/L, lagers 6–7, stouts 4–5. Too much = exploding bottles.
useCases: Homebrewer about to bottle a 19-liter (5-gallon) batch of American IPA fermented at 20°C wants to hit 2.5 volumes of CO2. The calc returns ~130 g of dextrose, or ~3.4 g per 500 ml bottle.

First-time bottler with a 23-liter Belgian Tripel fermented at 24°C targeting 3.5 volumes: the calc warns this needs ~245 g of dextrose and recommends using Belgian-style 33 cl bottles rated for the extra pressure.
Brewer who normally uses 130 g of dextrose ran out and only has table sugar (sucrose); the calc adjusts the equivalent to ~118 g (sucrose is 9% more efficient by mass).

A craft homebrewer wants to use 100 g of wildflower honey instead of dextrose for a saison to add a subtle floral note: the calc converts to honey factor 4.26 and recommends ~145 g for the same target volumes.

Bottle of last batch came out under-carbonated after 3 weeks: the calc helps diagnose by recomputing assumed residual CO2 against the actual fermentation temp (28°C ambient summer, not the 20°C originally entered).
A pub-style English bitter at 1.2 volumes: the calc returns just ~35 g of dextrose for a 23 L batch, producing the characteristic low-carbonation cask profile.

Brewing a high-gravity Belgian Dark Strong Ale at 4.0 volumes: the calc returns ~315 g but flags that this exceeds safe pressure for standard bottles and requires 33 cl champagne-style bottles with crown caps rated to 6 bar.
A brewer bulk-priming a 19 L keg for force carbonation reference: the calc gives the equivalent sugar amount to compare with the CO2 tank pressure-temperature chart for the target 2.5 volumes.
explanation:
## What Is Priming Sugar

When bottling, you add sugar that residual yeast consumes, generating CO₂ in the sealed bottle. This takes **2–3 weeks** at 68°F (20°C).

## CO₂ Volumes by Beer Style

| Style | Volumes |
|---|---|
| British Cask Ale | 1.0–1.5 |
| Porter, Stout | 1.7–2.3 |
| **American Ale, IPA** | **2.2–2.7** |
| Pilsner, Lager | 2.4–2.7 |
| Hefeweizen, Wheat | 3.3–4.5 |
| Belgian Tripel, Saison | 3.0–4.0 |

## The Formula

```
grams = (target_vol − residual_vol) × volume_L × factor

dextrose_factor = 3.86
table_sugar_factor = 3.51
DME_factor = 4.50
honey_factor = 4.26

residual_vol = 3.0378 − 0.050062 × T(°C) + 0.00026555 × T²
```

## Quick Reference for 20L

| Volumes | Dextrose | Table Sugar |
|---|---|---|
| 2.0 (stout) | 85g | 77g |
| **2.4 (IPA)** | **120g** | **110g** |
| 2.7 (pilsner) | 145g | 130g |
| 3.0 (wheat) | 170g | 155g |
| 3.5 (Belgian) | 205g | 185g |

## Warning: Bottle Bombs

>4 vol CO₂ in standard bottles has **explosion risk**. Use champagne or Belgian bottles for high carbonation.

## Common Mistakes

1. **Forget residual CO₂**: fermentation at 82°F (28°C) = 0.6 vol, at 59°F (15°C) = 1.1 vol.
2. **Don't boil the priming sugar**: make a 5-minute syrup to sterilize.
3. **Shaking when bottling**: oxidizes the beer.

See [final volume calculator](/calculadora-final-volume-cerveza-fermentador).

faq.q: What is the practical difference between dextrose, table sugar, DME, and honey for priming?
faq.a: All four ferment cleanly enough for priming, but they differ in efficiency, flavor impact, and ease of use. **Dextrose (corn sugar)** is the homebrewer standard: 100% fermentable, neutral flavor, factor 3.86 g/L per volume of CO2. **Table sugar (sucrose)** is ~91% as efficient per gram (you need 9% more by weight), but the yeast inverts it to glucose and fructose; flavor impact is negligible at priming doses. **DME (dry malt extract)** adds residual sweetness and a hint of malt body, plus a slight haze; factor ~4.50, slightly less efficient than dextrose. **Honey** adds a subtle floral note and is ~75-80% fermentable; factor ~4.26. For pure carbonation control with no flavor change, use dextrose. For sweetness retention in a sweet stout or Belgian dark, DME is preferred. Honey for saisons or braggots.

faq.q: How long does beer take to carbonate after bottle conditioning?
faq.a: Typically **2-3 weeks at room temperature (68°F / 20°C)** for standard ales and IPAs at 2.4-2.7 volumes of CO2. Cold conditioning at 50-60°F (10-15°C) takes 4-6 weeks because yeast metabolism slows down. High-gravity beers (over 8% ABV) like Belgian quads or barleywines can take 6-8 weeks because residual sugars and alcohol stress the yeast. After visible carbonation appears, an additional 1-2 weeks of cold conditioning at 38-45°F (3-7°C) improves clarity and lets the CO2 fully integrate, giving smaller bubbles and better head retention. If a bottle pours flat after 4 weeks at 68°F, suspect dead yeast, oxidized priming sugar, or under-pitched yeast at bottling.

faq.q: Can beer bottles really explode from over-carbonation?
faq.a: **Yes, and it is a real safety hazard**. Standard 12 oz beer bottles are rated to roughly 50-60 PSI (3.4-4.1 bar), which corresponds to about 3.5-4.0 volumes of CO2 at 68°F. Above 4 volumes in standard bottles, the risk of bottle bombs increases sharply: glass shards can fly several meters at high velocity. For high-carbonation styles (Belgian tripels, saisons, wheat beers above 4.0 vol), use Belgian-style 33 cl bottles with crown caps or champagne-style 75 cl bottles with cages and corks, both rated to 90-130 PSI (6-9 bar). Also be aware of **secondary fermentation surprises**: if you bottle a beer that hasn't truly finished fermenting (FG above expected), residual unfermented sugars will continue to convert to CO2 and overshoot your target. Always verify final gravity is stable across 3 consecutive days before bottling.

faq.q: Do I need to boil the priming sugar before adding it to the beer?
faq.a: **Yes, always**. Dissolve the priming sugar in 1-2 cups of water and **boil it gently for 5-10 minutes** to sterilize and dissolve completely. Sugar straight from the bag is not sterile and can carry wild yeast, mold spores, or bacteria (especially raw sugars and honey, which can contain *Clostridium botulinum* spores, though the alcohol in beer normally prevents botulinum growth — sterilization is for general infection control, not botulism specifically). Cool the syrup to within 5°C of the beer temperature before adding, to avoid temperature shock to the yeast. Add the syrup to the bottling bucket first, then gently rack the beer on top to ensure even mixing without splashing (which introduces oxygen and causes oxidation/stale flavors).

faq.q: What CO2 volumes should different beer styles have?
faq.a: From the **BJCP 2021 style guidelines**: **British cask ales** 1.0-1.5 volumes; **British bitters, milds, brown ales** 1.5-2.0; **stouts and porters** 1.7-2.3; **American ales, IPAs, pale ales** 2.2-2.7; **German pilsners and continental lagers** 2.4-2.7; **wheat beers (hefeweizen, witbier)** 3.3-4.5; **Belgian tripels, dubbels, blondes** 2.5-3.5; **Belgian saisons** 3.0-4.0; **Belgian lambics and gueuze** 3.0-4.5; **American IPAs (hazy/NEIPA)** 2.2-2.6 (lower than West Coast IPA, ~2.5 typically). Highly carbonated styles need stronger bottles and longer conditioning. Bock and dunkel sit at 2.4-2.8. Imperial stouts often go lower at 1.8-2.4 to highlight roast malt and avoid hiding alcohol with fizz.

faq.q: What is residual CO2 and why does it matter for priming calculations?
faq.a: **Residual CO2** is the carbon dioxide already dissolved in the beer at the moment of bottling, naturally generated during primary fermentation. The amount depends almost entirely on **temperature**: cold beer holds more CO2 in solution (Henry's law). At 32°F (0°C) beer holds ~1.7 volumes of residual CO2; at 50°F (10°C) ~1.2 vol; at 68°F (20°C) ~0.85 vol; at 75°F (24°C) ~0.72 vol; at 86°F (30°C) ~0.55 vol. The Palmer equation is `residual = 3.0378 − 0.050062 × T(°C) + 0.00026555 × T²`. You must **subtract the residual from your target** to compute the CO2 you actually need to generate with priming sugar. Forgetting this is one of the most common over-carbonation mistakes: a brewer fermenting cool at 60°F and bottling without accounting for ~1 volume already in solution can easily overshoot by 0.5+ volumes.

faq.q: Why did my beer come out flat after 3 weeks of conditioning?
faq.a: Several likely causes, in order of frequency: **(1) Cold conditioning room** — at temperatures below 60°F (15°C), yeast metabolism slows dramatically; move bottles to a 68-72°F closet for 1-2 more weeks. **(2) Dead or stressed yeast at bottling** — high alcohol (>9% ABV), low pitching rate, prolonged secondary fermentation, or aging in cold for months can leave too few viable yeast cells to carbonate; consider re-pitching with a small dose of fresh dry yeast (~0.1 g/L). **(3) Bad bottle seals** — verify crown caps are tight; squeeze gently, you shouldn't hear hissing. **(4) Insufficient priming sugar** — recompute with the calc and adjust on next batch. **(5) Yeast killed by sanitizer** — residual Star San or iodophor in the bottling bucket can stress yeast. After ruling out these, wait 4 more weeks; some high-gravity beers simply take 6-8 weeks to carbonate.

faq.q: Can I use honey instead of dextrose for priming, and what's the conversion?
faq.a: **Yes**. Honey is approximately 75-80% fermentable by yeast (the rest is non-fermentable polysaccharides and water), so you need about **10-15% more honey by weight** than dextrose for the same CO2 output. The Palmer factor is ~4.26 versus 3.86 for dextrose. Honey also imparts a **subtle floral or earthy note** depending on the variety (clover honey is neutral, wildflower more pronounced, buckwheat very strong). It works particularly well in saisons, braggots, and Belgian wits. Avoid using honey for priming in styles where you want a clean, malt-forward flavor (pilsners, English bitters), as even small amounts of priming honey can shift the character. Always boil honey briefly to sterilize and to drive off any volatile flavor compounds you don't want.

faq.q: Should I prime each bottle individually or bulk-prime in a bottling bucket?
faq.a: **Bulk-priming is strongly preferred** by serious homebrewers and commercial bottle-conditioned breweries. Method: dissolve all your priming sugar in 1-2 cups of boiled water, pour into a sanitized bottling bucket, then gently rack (siphon) the beer from primary on top of the syrup. Stir very gently with a sanitized spoon. This ensures **even sugar distribution** across all bottles and consistent carbonation. Per-bottle priming (1 teaspoon per 22 oz bottle, etc.) is error-prone: even small variation in tablet/spoon size produces wildly different carbonation levels across bottles, and the wide opening exposes more bottles to oxygen. Pre-measured priming tabs (carbonation drops) work fine for small batches or one-off bottles but cost more per dose and offer less precision.

faq.q: How does altitude affect priming sugar calculations?
faq.a: **Significantly for some homebrewers**. CO2 volumes are defined at 1 atmosphere (sea level, 1013 hPa). At higher elevations, atmospheric pressure is lower, so the partial pressure of CO2 driving dissolution into the beer is lower. **Practically: at 1,500 m (Mexico City, Bogotá, Denver, Quito), you may perceive 5-8% less carbonation than the same beer at sea level**, all else equal. To compensate, increase priming sugar by ~7% at 1,500 m or by 12-15% at 3,000+ m (La Paz, El Alto). The math: at 3,500 m, atmospheric pressure is ~660 hPa vs 1013 hPa at sea level (~65%). Most online priming calculators (including this one) assume sea level; if you're brewing in the Andes, the Alps, or Colorado, adjust upward. Conversely, if you carbonate in a keg at altitude, the gauge pressure shows higher CO2 than the actual dissolved level.

faq.q: Is force carbonation in a keg better than bottle conditioning?
faq.a: **It depends on your goals**. Force carbonation (using a CO2 tank and keg) is **faster (2-4 days vs 2-3 weeks)**, **more precise** (you control PSI/temp directly), and avoids the sediment that forms at the bottom of bottle-conditioned beer. Most American craft breweries force-carbonate for these reasons. However, **bottle conditioning preserves natural yeast in suspension**, which improves long-term shelf stability and creates the traditional flavor profile of Belgian Trappist beers, English real ales, and German hefeweizens. Many style purists also argue bottle-conditioned beer has smaller, creamier bubbles. If you brew styles where authenticity matters (Belgian, traditional German, English cask), use bottle conditioning. If you brew styles where freshness and consistency matter (American IPA, lager, pilsner), force carbonation in a keg is usually preferred.

faq.q: How do I store bottle-conditioned beer for the long term?
faq.a: **Store upright, in the dark, at cool temperatures (38-55°F / 3-13°C)**. Light, especially blue-spectrum and UV, breaks down hop iso-alpha acids into 3-methylbut-2-ene-1-thiol ("skunky" compound), so brown glass is preferred and clear/green glass should be kept in a closed cabinet. Heat above 70°F accelerates staling and oxidation. Most session-strength ales and IPAs are best fresh and decline after 3-6 months; **hop character fades fastest**. Strong beers (over 8% ABV, like Belgian quads, barleywines, imperial stouts, lambics) **age well for 1-5+ years** and develop complex sherry, dried fruit, and leather notes. Always store upright after the first week of conditioning so the yeast sediment compacts cleanly at the bottom and you can pour clear beer at serving time.
